plannerAnswers.question: What did you like most about this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: How concrete it is about the place the work happens. The 'This computer' section and 'What this computer doesn't have' list the real browsers, tools, ports and stand-ins for a pad, touch, a second player and a TV, so I could test claims instead of guessing. I also liked the split between a high bar (complete, no stubs, a whole-game playthrough) and real freedom (genre, perspective, effort, an unlimited performance budget), and that the engine and hub are public and runnable, so a plan can be checked against them before anyone builds from it.

plannerAnswers.question: What was confusing?
plannerAnswers.answer: Four things. (1) 'Follow the hub doc for multiplayer integration into ai-hub as well as for the game on its own': the hub protocol has no multiplayer outside a session, only connect() returning null and the game running alone. I planned it that way, with solo play and optional AI teammates, and said so in the plan, but the sentence could also mean a second network path. (2) TASK.md says 'pick' for genre, perspective and research, while the stage asks me to plan for builders who also read those lines. I decided that the plan settles them, except the title, and told builders so at the top. (3) 'Leave out TASK.md's file and folder names' does not say whether that covers the exit interview file. I left every file name out and described each one instead. (4) The engine's game guide and README point at labs/playground as the worked example, but new-game does not copy that folder into the workspace, so a builder has to know to keep the clone.

plannerAnswers.question: What was the hardest thing to do?
plannerAnswers.answer: Two things. The creative one was carrying the source's mechanics (planted aim, body-part reactions into a kick, a grid inventory, a merchant economy, an escort, campy villains) with no recreation of its characters, story, levels or music, at a scope a builder of unknown capability can finish with nothing stubbed. That is why the plan has an always-shippable build order and an explicit cut order. The technical one was that the worst problems only appear in combination, so only running spikes found them: the hub's ?aihub=1 query stops createEngine from starting; inlined dynamic imports run eagerly in the one-file build; the harness allows only 20 s for ready() across four software-rendered WebGPU copies; the full Chromium binary crashes under the run's long temp path, while the headless shell works.

plannerAnswers.question: What would you change in this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: I would say plainly whether multiplayer outside the hub is wanted. I would put the working CHROMIUM_PATH line and 'skip scripts/setup.sh' in 'This computer'. I would add to the hub or engine docs that my-3dge games must strip aihub* query keys before createEngine, and state the harness's 20 s ready limit in the protocol page, since a WebGPU game can easily miss it. I would ask the engine to offer a one-file build for games, not only for its playground. I would tell the planner which models and budgets the builders will have, so scope can be set on purpose rather than hedged with a cut order. And I would state whether the plan may override choices TASK.md gives to 'you'.
